questions.question: Sound waves enter our ears and cause parts of our auditory system to vibrate. Which sequence correctly shows the order in which these parts vibrate?
options: Eardrum, tiny bones, and the cochlea
Cochlea, eardrum, and tiny bones
Tiny bones, cochlea, and eardrum
Eardrum, cochlea, and nerve cells

questions.question: Where are the specialised cells that sense vibrations and cause electrical signals to be sent along a nerve to the brain located?
options: Inside the outer ear canal
On the surface of the eardrum
Inside the cochlea
Along the auditory tube

questions.question: How does the brain create the sensation of hearing a sound?
options: By receiving mechanical vibrations directly from the skull bones
By receiving electrical signals from the ear through a nerve
By sensing the changes in air pressure inside the skull
By sending electrical signals back to the eardrum to make it vibrate

questions.question: What is the range of sound frequencies that a healthy human ear can typically detect, and in which range is it most sensitive?
options: 20 Hz to 20 kHz, being most sensitive to 2-5 kHz waves
10 Hz to 10 kHz, being most sensitive to 1-3 kHz waves
50 Hz to 50 kHz, being most sensitive to 5-10 kHz waves
20 Hz to 20,000 kHz, being most sensitive to 20-50 Hz waves

questions.question: Which of the following describes sounds that are outside the range of human hearing because their frequencies are either too low or too high?
options: Infrasound is below 20 Hz, and ultrasound is above 20 kHz
Ultrasound is below 20 Hz, and infrasound is above 20 kHz
Infrasound is below 2 Hz, and ultrasound is above 200 kHz
Ultrasound is below 200 Hz, and infrasound is above 20,000 Hz

questions.question: How are sound waves produced when an object, like a drum skin, vibrates?
options: The vibrating object creates a vacuum that pulls air particles along with it
The vibrating object causes nearby air particles to vibrate as well
The vibrating object heats up the air, creating thermal currents
The vibrating object shoots out air particles in all directions

questions.question: When a sound wave travels through the air, what happens to the individual air particles?
options: They travel all the way from the source of the sound to the listener's ear
They spin in small circles but do not move back and forth
They vibrate parallel to the direction of wave travel, not travelling forwards
They vibrate up and down at right angles to the direction the sound is travelling

questions.question: Why is sound classified as a longitudinal wave?
options: Because the air particles vibrate at a right angle to the direction of energy transfer
Because the wave can only travel over very long distances
Because the direction of vibration is parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Because the speed of the wave increases as the wavelength gets longer

questions.question: Why do sound waves travel faster in liquids and solids than they do in gases?
options: Because the particles are very close, so vibrations are easily passed on
Because liquids and solids are much warmer than gases
Because particles in liquids and solids have less mass than gas particles
Because waves in liquids and solids are transverse rather than longitudinal

questions.question: Why does sound travel even faster in solids than in liquids?
options: Solids have weaker forces between particles, letting them slide easily
The strong forces between particles in a solid mean vibrations travel even faster
Particles in a solid are free to move around and carry the energy directly
Solid particles are much larger than liquid particles

questions.question: What is meant by the term 'speed of sound'?
options: The time it takes for a single air particle to travel one metre
The distance travelled by a sound wave pulse every second
The number of vibrations that pass a fixed point each second
The maximum distance a particle moves from its rest position

questions.question: Which of the following lists the correct approximate speed of sound in air, and how its speed changes in different states?
options: About 340 m/s in air, faster in liquids and faster still in solids
About 340 m/s in air, slower in liquids and slowest in solids
About 1500 m/s in air, slower in liquids and faster in solids
About 340 m/s in air, and it cannot travel through liquids or solids

questions.question: What physical phenomenon occurs when sound waves reflect off a hard surface, travel back, and are heard again?
options: Refraction
Dispersion
An echo
Resonance

questions.question: A student stands 170 metres away from a large wall and claps. The sound of the clap reflects off the wall and returns as an echo in 1.0 second. What is the calculated speed of sound?
options: 85 m/s

questions.question: In an experiment to measure the speed of sound, why is it better to measure longer distances and times?
options: It makes the sound wave travel faster through the air
It means any measurement errors are a smaller proportion of the measurements
It prevents the sound wave from reflecting off nearby objects
It increases the frequency of the sound waves being measured

questions.question: Which of the following defines ultrasound waves?
options: Sound waves with a frequency below 20 Hz that humans cannot hear
Sound waves with a frequency above 20 000 Hz that humans cannot hear
Sound waves that travel faster than the speed of light
Sound waves with a very high amplitude that can cause hearing damage

questions.question: How is ultrasound used to image structures inside the human body?
options: It heats up different tissues to create a thermal map
It reflects from boundaries between different tissues
It ionises the cells to produce a highly detailed X-ray image
It is absorbed completely by bones, leaving a shadow on film

questions.question: What is the movement of water particles as a water wave moves forward?
options: Each bit of water moves forward along with the wave
Each bit of water is moving up and down (oscillating), not forward
Each bit of water moves in a continuous figure-of-eight pattern forward
Each bit of water remains completely still while only energy moves

questions.question: Why are water waves classified as transverse waves?
options: Because the direction of oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Because the direction of oscillation is 90 degrees to the direction of energy transfer
Because they can only travel through a vacuum
Because they transfer matter instead of transferring energy

questions.question: How is the amplitude of a water wave defined?
options: The total distance from the very bottom of a trough to the very top of a crest
The greatest distance water moves above and below the rest position
The number of complete waves that pass a point in one second
The distance from one wave crest to the very next wave crest
